dayTitle: Two thousand seven hundred kilograms short
title: What the loop settles at
task: Match each change to the loop with what it does to the methane at equilibrium.
scene: The loading projection is still 2,700 kilograms short. Herrera has stopped accepting slogans like ‘run it hotter.’ Four proposed changes are on the reactor board. He wants each effect agreed before anyone touches the loop.
takeaway: Pressure, temperature, product removal and an inert gas do not disturb an equilibrium in the same way.
why: Each of these is the same principle applied to a different quantity. Pressure counts gas molecules, and five go in where three come out, so squeezing the loop favours the smaller side. Temperature is different in kind: heat is one of the products here, so the equilibrium constant itself falls as the bed is heated. Condensing the water changes the ratio without touching the constant. Argon raises the total pressure and no partial pressure, so the mixture never notices that it is there.
assumes: a reaction at equilibrium is still running in both directions
pressure and temperature are the two settings on a gas-phase reactor

choices: More methane: the forward direction ends with fewer gas molecules than it starts with.
Less methane: the assembly gives out heat, and supplying more heat pushes it back.
More methane: taking an output away leaves the mixture short of the ratio it settles at.
No change: nothing taking part in the reaction has had its own partial pressure altered.
scenarios: The loop pressure is raised from eight bar to twelve.
The bed is run forty degrees hotter at the same pressure.
Product water is condensed out before the gas returns to the inlet.
Argon builds up in the loop, raising the total pressure at fixed volume.

equations.about: reading which way a mixture will move from what is in it now

dayTitle: Two thousand seven hundred kilograms short
title: Rate is not yield
task: Say what forty degrees actually buys
scene: Sundqvist wants the bed at 320 °C tonight, up from 280. Ravneet Kaur, the catalysis engineer, has the temperature profile and the production projection side by side. One setting may rescue the schedule or deepen the shortfall.
question: The bed is run forty degrees hotter at the same pressure and the same flow. What happens?
takeaway: Temperature can increase reaction rate while decreasing the equilibrium yield of an exothermic reaction.
why: Temperature moves two different quantities in opposite directions. The rate constant rises because more collisions can clear the activation barrier. That is a kinetic effect. For this exothermic reaction, the equilibrium constant falls as temperature rises. That is a thermodynamic effect. A hotter bed can therefore reach a lower methane ceiling more quickly. Whether the trade helps depends on recycle, residence time and how much unreacted feed the loop can send around again.
assumes: heating a reaction makes it go faster
an exothermic reaction gives out heat as it proceeds

choices: The bed turns gas over faster, and the methane a single pass can give falls a little.
Both the speed and the amount at equilibrium rise together, since heat helps a reaction along.
The speed is unchanged and the yield rises, since the catalyst is what sets the pace.
Neither moves much, since loop pressure is what fixes the speed and the amount alike.
rebuttals: Heat helps the rate and hinders the balance, and treating the two as one quantity is the mistake this reactor keeps making.
A catalyst changes how quickly the balance is reached and leaves the balance itself where it was.
Pressure does move this equilibrium, and it is not what sets the rate constant.

dayTitle: Two thousand seven hundred kilograms short
title: What freezes before methane condenses
task: Say why the stream is cleaned before it is cooled
scene: The cold line takes the product stream from ten degrees down to a hundred and fifteen kelvin in one run of pipe. Mei-Ling Cho, the cryogenics engineer, will not accept a stream that has skipped the drier.
question: Why does the stream pass a drier and a carbon dioxide trap before it reaches the cold line?
takeaway: A cold line is a series of temperatures, and every substance in the stream leaves the gas at its own one.
why: Every substance in the stream leaves the gas phase at its own temperature. Water freezes near 273 K. Carbon dioxide can deposit directly as a solid near 195 K at these pressures. Methane remains gaseous until the stream is much colder, near its condensation temperature. If water and carbon dioxide are not removed first, both can become solids on exchanger surfaces. A growing solid layer narrows the passage and can mimic a valve or refrigeration fault from outside the pipe.
assumes: a substance leaves the gas phase at a temperature that depends on the pressure
liquid methane needs about 112 K at loop pressure

choices: Water and carbon dioxide turn solid at temperatures the line passes through on its way down.
Water and carbon dioxide dissolve into the liquid methane and cannot be separated afterwards.
Both gases carry heat into the cold end and raise the load on the refrigerator.
The drier and the trap are what raise the pressure the cold line needs to work at.
rebuttals: Neither one gets as far as the liquid methane; both are solid on the wall well before that.
The heat they carry is real and small, and it is not what closes the line.
Both fittings take a small pressure drop rather than adding pressure.

title: How long a molecule stays in the bed
task: Work out how long the gas is in contact with the catalyst
scene: Kaur wants the contact time worked out at the new flow before anything else is changed. The bed holds three hundred and forty litres of packed catalyst and the loop is passing eighty-five litres a minute through it.
question: Estimate how long a molecule of gas spends inside the bed.
takeaway: Conversion depends on how fast the reaction runs and on how long it is allowed to run for.
why: Residence time is the contact the reaction gets. A rate constant says how quickly reaction occurs at the stated conditions. Residence time says how long the gas remains with the catalyst. Conversion depends on both. Raising throughput by pushing more gas through the same bed shortens that contact. The plant can therefore increase flow while lowering conversion in one move. Rate and residence time must be judged together before a higher production setting is accepted.
assumes: a flow quoted in litres a minute is a volume passing each minute
gas volumes depend on the pressure and temperature they are quoted at

estimate.prompt: The bed holds 340 litres of packed catalyst, and the loop passes 85 litres a minute through it at reactor conditions.
estimate.question: Estimate how long a molecule of gas spends inside the bed.
estimate.relationship: Residence time = the volume of the packed bed ÷ the gas flow through it each minute, with both measured at the reactor's own pressure and temperature.
estimate.explanation: Contact time is the bed's volume divided by the flow through it. The pressure and the temperature are already inside that flow figure, which is quoted at reactor conditions.
labels: 85 L/min  (flow through the bed at reactor conditions)
4  (moles of hydrogen per mole of carbon dioxide)
givens: Gas flow 85 L/min at reactor conditions

equations.about: how long the reaction is given to happen in

title: Which electrode does which job
task: Match each part of the cell to what it does.
scene: The hall runs two kinds of cell: one splits water, the other splits carbon dioxide at eight hundred degrees. Rosalind Achebe, the power and electrolysis engineer, has the four parts listed on the board.
takeaway: The two halves of one electron transfer can be run in separate places if something carries an ion between them.
why: Electrolysis separates the two halves of one electron-transfer reaction. Electrons enter at the cathode, where reduction occurs. Electrons leave at the anode, where oxidation occurs. The solid electrolyte carries ions between those regions without carrying electrons through the same path. That separation keeps oxygen away from the fuel-side product. Current measures how quickly charge is delivered through the external circuit. Faraday’s law then connects the total charge passed to the maximum amount of product the cell can make.
assumes: oxidation is loss of electrons and reduction is gain of electrons
a current is a flow of charge

choices: Reduction: carbon dioxide takes up electrons here and leaves an oxide ion behind.
Oxidation: oxide ions give up electrons here and depart as oxygen gas.
It carries oxide ions across and refuses to carry electrons, so the circuit runs through the wire.
It fixes how many moles a sol the cell can make, since charge and moles are proportional.
scenarios: The cathode, where the supply pushes electrons into the stream.
The anode, where electrons are pulled back out.
The solid electrolyte between them.
The setting on the power supply.

equations.about: Faraday's law: charge into kilograms

title: What has to be paid for
task: State which of the plant's steps have a bill
scene: Demir has the sol’s energy ledger open on the desk. The reactor releases heat while it runs, while electrolysis takes most of the array output. He wants the difference stated plainly in the log.
question: Why does splitting water need a power supply while the methane assembly does not?
takeaway: Whether a change runs on its own and how fast it goes are two separate questions, and one of them has a bill.
why: Direction is set by the free-energy change, which weighs the heat given out against the change in how spread out the matter is. Assembling methane from carbon dioxide and hydrogen gives out a great deal of heat and runs downhill. Splitting water is that same reaction backwards: it takes the energy in, and no arrangement of equipment gets out of paying it. Electricity is how the plant pays. A catalyst can make a downhill change fast, and cannot make an uphill change run.
assumes: some reactions give out heat and others take it in
electrical energy can be counted in kilowatt-hours

choices: Splitting water raises the free energy of what comes out, and that has to be supplied.
Splitting water is the slower of the two, and a slow reaction needs power to keep it going.
Water is a liquid, and turning a liquid into two gases is what the electricity pays for.
The assembly has a catalyst, and a catalyst supplies the energy a reaction would need.
rebuttals: Speed and direction are different properties, and a fast uphill reaction still has to be driven.
Boiling the water would cost far less than splitting it, and the plant is not boiling anything.
A catalyst opens an easier path and puts no energy in; it leaves the free-energy change exactly where it was.

dayTitle: The line that stopped passing gas
title: Find where the cold line is closing
task: Walk the cold line, take the readings that localise the first abnormal section, and name what is building there.
scene: Cold-line flow is still falling. Cho has the isolation valves ready, but shutting the wrong section costs another production cycle. The cold head is holding set point while pressure continues to rise upstream of the exchanger.
question: Where does the normal pattern first break, and what is closing the line?
takeaway: A blockage is localised by the first place pressure, flow or composition departs from the normal chain.
why: The cold head is at set point, so the refrigerator is still producing the required temperature. Jacket pressure is also steady, which argues against lost insulation. The abnormal evidence begins upstream: pressure rises while flow falls over hours rather than stopping at once. The drier outlet also carries 900 ppm water. That water reaches a section cold enough to freeze and accumulates as ice. A shut valve would produce a sudden stop. A growing plug produces the slow pressure-and-flow pattern seen here.
assumes: a refrigerator that has reached its set point is doing its job
water freezes at a far higher temperature than methane condenses at
answerText: The restriction is forming in the exchanger after the drier. Water at about 900 ppm is reaching the cold section and freezing into a growing plug.

choices: Water past the drier is freezing in the exchanger
The refrigerator has lost capacity since the hot run began
The vacuum jacket has failed
A valve on the cold line was left shut
choiceMechanisms: The line cools through 273 K long before it gets anywhere near methane.
A cold head short of temperature passes gas where it should deliver liquid.
Heat leaking in warms the line and stops it condensing anything.
A closed valve blocks the flow with everything else reading normally.
text.headline: The cold line stopped passing gas over three hours, with the refrigerator at temperature.

data.hint: Start at the warm end and move downstream. Read only enough points to find the first place the normal pressure-and-flow pattern stops matching the reference run.

stages.label: Exchanger inlet
stages.reading: Upstream pressure rising while flow falls over hours
stages.reference: Pressure and flow steady on a clean run

stages.label: Tank-side flow
stages.reference: Tracks inlet flow on a clean line

why_this_format: The old diagnosis let the player choose “ice blockage” from a list. PROBE makes the player move along the process chain and locate the first abnormal section before naming the mechanism.
trap_is_satisfied_by: No new numerical threshold is invented. The authored evidence already fixes the pattern: cold-head temperature and jacket pressure stay normal while upstream pressure rises, flow declines over hours, and the drier outlet carries 900 ppm water.
player_does: probe the drier outlet, exchanger inlet, cold head and jacket
identify the first point where the reference pattern fails
name the material that can accumulate at that location

failure_feedback.action: blaming the refrigerator because the downstream flow is low
failure_feedback.consequence: the cold head is still at set point, so replacing it leaves the growing restriction untouched
failure_feedback.line: The cold end is cold. Find where the pressure starts piling up.

dayTitle: The line that stopped passing gas
title: Why the hotter pass gave less
task: Separate the thermodynamic temperature effect from the flow change in the hot run.
scene: The hot run’s assay is on Herrera’s desk. Conversion per pass fell from 71% to 64% while throughput rose. He wants the reason written down before anyone argues for another temperature increase.
question: What happened to the equilibrium methane ceiling when temperature rose, even though the observed conversion may also reflect shorter residence time?
takeaway: Heating an exothermic reaction lowers its equilibrium product yield, while the observed reactor conversion can also depend on kinetics and residence time.
why: The hot run changed two things at once: temperature rose and throughput increased. Those changes should not be collapsed into one explanation. Thermodynamically, the higher temperature lowers the equilibrium constant for this exothermic reaction and therefore lowers the methane ceiling. Kinetically, the hotter catalyst reacts faster, while the higher flow shortens residence time. The observed 64% conversion can contain both effects. A later controlled flow test can separate them by changing residence time while holding temperature and pressure fixed.
assumes: the equilibrium constant is fixed at a given temperature
the Sabatier reaction gives out heat

choices: The equilibrium methane ceiling is lower at the higher temperature, even though the rate constant is larger.
The equilibrium ceiling is higher because hotter molecules collide more often and reach products more easily.
Temperature leaves equilibrium unchanged; only the shorter residence time can lower conversion.
The catalyst changes the equilibrium constant when it becomes hotter, so the balance follows catalyst activity.
rebuttals: Collision frequency and activation energy affect rate, not the direction in which an exothermic equilibrium shifts with temperature.
Residence time can affect the measured conversion, but the equilibrium constant also changes with temperature.
A catalyst changes how fast equilibrium is reached and does not set the equilibrium constant.

equations.about: reading which way a mixture will move from what is in it now

dayTitle: The line that stopped passing gas
title: Getting water out of frozen ground
task: Order the steps the water plant runs in.
scene: Femi Abiola, the regolith and water lead, has the plant’s four steps written on cards. The morning crew disagreed about where the extra water appeared. He wants the cards restored to process order.
takeaway: Every step in the water plant fixes something the step after it cannot survive.
why: The order is set by what each step needs from the one above it. Ice that melts in the bucket runs into the ground and is lost, so the load stays frozen until it is inside something sealed. Vapour has to be captured where it is released or it goes into the atmosphere at six millibars. Condensing gives liquid water, and only liquid water can be run through an ion-exchange bed. Take the steps out of order and each one has nothing to work on.
assumes: warming ice-bearing soil releases water as vapour at low pressure
dissolved salts stay behind when water evaporates

cards: Cut ice-bearing ground and keep the load below its melting point on the way in.
Warm a sealed hopper so the water leaves the soil as vapour with nowhere else to go.
Condense that vapour on a chilled plate and drain it into a holding tank.
Strip chloride out on the polishing column at the outlet of the holding tank.

dayTitle: The loop that pays for itself
title: How much gas the bed has to be fed
task: Size the carbon dioxide the bed needs each sol
scene: The plant has to average thirteen point eight kilograms of methane a sol from here to the window. Herrera wants the carbon dioxide that implies before the intake compressors are asked for anything.
question: Estimate the carbon dioxide the reactor must be fed each sol.
takeaway: Stoichiometry turns a production target into a feed rate, and the feed rate is what the intake has to meet.
why: Stoichiometry is mole bookkeeping. The balanced reaction sends one carbon atom from each carbon-dioxide molecule into one methane molecule. Mass adds one conversion step. Carbon dioxide has a molar mass of 44 g/mol, while methane is 16 g/mol. Each kilogram of methane therefore needs 44/16 kilograms of carbon dioxide. The intake compressors must gather that feed from a very thin atmosphere. The required compressor work scales directly with the production target the plant promises to meet.
assumes: one mole of carbon dioxide yields one mole of methane in this reaction
a molar mass converts moles to kilograms

estimate.prompt: The plant must average 13.8 kg of methane a sol. One mole of carbon dioxide gives one mole of methane.
estimate.question: Estimate the carbon dioxide the reactor must be fed each sol.
estimate.relationship: Feed mass = product mass × the molar mass of the feed ÷ the molar mass of the product, when the two are consumed and made in equal numbers of moles.
estimate.explanation: Equal moles of the two gases, so the mass ratio is the ratio of the molar masses. The hydrogen and the water are elsewhere in the ledger.
estimate.solution: 13.8 kg × 44.0 ÷ 16.0 = 37.9 kg of carbon dioxide a sol.
labels: 4  (moles of hydrogen per mole of carbon dioxide)
2  (moles of water made per mole of methane)

equations.e: CO₂ + 4H₂ → CH₄ + 2H₂O,  ΔH = −165 kJ per mole
equations.about: the reaction the whole plant is built around

dayTitle: The loop that pays for itself
title: Where eight per cent of the charge went
task: Close the hydrogen-equivalent charge ledger and identify the part of the current that did not become collected hydrogen.
scene: The cell held 640 amps for a full sol. Faraday’s law predicts about 594 grams of hydrogen, but the separator collected only 546. Achebe has already checked the collection-line pressure and the hydrogen inventory downstream.
question: What term closes the charge ledger, and what does that term measure about the cell?
takeaway: Faraday’s law fixes the theoretical product from charge; current efficiency measures how much of that charge reached the intended reaction.
why: Current times time gives charge, and Faraday’s law converts that charge into a theoretical hydrogen mass. For this run the charge corresponds to about 594 grams. Only 546 grams were collected, while line inventory and measured vent loss were unchanged. The missing 48 grams are therefore not a hidden hydrogen store. They are hydrogen-equivalent charge that crossed by other electrochemical paths or recombined before collection. The ratio 546/594 is about 92%, which is the current efficiency for this run.
assumes: Faraday’s law converts charge into a theoretical amount of product
current efficiency is collected product divided by theoretical product from charge
answerText: The ledger is short by about 48 g of hydrogen-equivalent charge. The cell collected 546/594 ≈ 92% of the Faraday-law maximum, so its current efficiency is about 92%.

choices: Some of the charge crossed the cell by a path that split no water.
The hydrogen was made and then leaked out of the collection line at low pressure.
Faraday's constant shifts with temperature, so the calculation overstates a hot stack.
The current meter reads high when the electrolyte warms up during a long run.
rebuttals: A leak downstream of the cell is worth checking and would show as pressure loss in the line, which this stack does not have.
The charge on a mole of electrons is fixed and does not depend on how warm the cell is.
A meter reading high would make the shortfall worse rather than explain it, since the true charge would be lower.

equations.about: Faraday's law: charge into kilograms

streams.label: Change in hydrogen held in the collection line
Charge not recovered as collected H₂

data.hint: All rows are written in hydrogen-equivalent grams. Count the measured product and any real downstream storage or loss before deciding what must be assigned to the cell itself.

why_this_format: A multiple choice asks for a label. BALANCE forces the player to reconcile measured charge with collected product and discover current efficiency as the missing term in a closed ledger.
trap_is_satisfied_by: The authored 8% shortfall makes the charge-equivalent total 594 g and the collected amount about 546 g. The visible streams sum to 546 g, not 594; adding the hidden 48 g-equivalent term closes the ledger exactly.

count collected hydrogen and checked downstream terms
close the missing 48 g-equivalent and report the 92% current efficiency

failure_feedback.consequence: the line pressure and inventory checks show no downstream loss, so the ledger still does not close
failure_feedback.line: A leak is a mass loss. Show me the mass loss.

dayTitle: The loop that pays for itself
title: What comes with the water
task: Match each dissolved species to what it does downstream.
scene: The holding tank's analysis is on Abiola's bench: four dissolved species, none of them water. Each one has somewhere downstream that it matters, and the plant has one polishing column between them and everything else.
takeaway: Water from the ground is a solution, and every solute has an address downstream.
why: A dissolved species matters because of the surface or process it reaches downstream. Chloride is dangerous here because it can bind strongly to nickel catalyst sites. Sulphate can contribute to scale on hot surfaces. Fine particles create a mechanical fouling problem. Dissolved carbon dioxide is different because the plant already handles carbon dioxide as a process species. The polishing train should therefore be designed around consequences, not around the idea that every impurity is equally harmful.
assumes: salts dissolve into ions in water
an electrolysis cell and a catalyst bed both have surfaces that can be fouled

choices: Binds to the nickel surface of the catalyst and takes those sites out of use.
Comes out of solution as scale on the hot faces of the electrolysis cell.
Packs into the drier and raises the pressure drop across it sol by sol.
Adds acidity and nothing else; the reactor is fed the same gas anyway.
scenarios: Chloride ion, from dissolved perchlorate salt.
Sulphate ion, at four grams a litre.
Suspended fines, too small for the filter.
Dissolved carbon dioxide, from the condenser headspace.

title: The temperature the reaction stops wanting to run
task: Work out the free-energy change at the bed's temperature
scene: Demir has thermodynamic data for the Sabatier reaction on the desk. The sheet lists its enthalpy and entropy changes per mole of methane. He wants ΔG evaluated at the present bed temperature.
question: Estimate the free-energy change for the reaction at the bed's temperature.
takeaway: With fixed tabulated ΔH and ΔS, ΔG = ΔH − TΔS predicts the temperature where spontaneity changes sign.
why: The enthalpy and entropy terms oppose each other. Methanation releases heat, which favours products, but it also reduces the number of gas molecules and gives a negative entropy change. The TΔS term therefore becomes more important as temperature rises. At 593 K the estimate is still strongly negative. Using the same tabulated ΔH and ΔS gives a zero crossing near 960 K. Real thermodynamic values vary somewhat with temperature, so 960 K is a course-model threshold rather than an exact plant limit.
assumes: free energy combines the heat of a reaction with its entropy change
a negative free-energy change means the reaction can run on its own

estimate.prompt: For this reaction the enthalpy change is −165,000 J per mole and the entropy change is −172 J per mole per kelvin. The bed is at 593 K.
estimate.question: Estimate the free-energy change for the reaction at the bed's temperature.
estimate.relationship: ΔG = ΔH − TΔS, with ΔG the free-energy change, ΔH the heat given out at constant pressure, T the absolute temperature in kelvin and ΔS the entropy change of the reaction.
estimate.explanation: Both terms are negative, and they pull opposite ways once the temperature multiplies the second. The gas constant and room temperature belong to other calculations.

equations.e: CO₂ + 4H₂ → CH₄ + 2H₂O,  ΔH = −165 kJ per mole
equations.about: the reaction the whole plant is built around

title: Same ceiling, different time
task: Sweep residence time for the standard and faster catalyst, then decide what the catalyst changed.
scene: Kaur has a standard charge and a higher-activity candidate at the same temperature and pressure. Sundqvist says the better catalyst should raise the methane ceiling. Kaur gives the player the flow control instead of answering him.
question: As contact time increases, what changes between the two charges, and what stays the same?
takeaway: A catalyst changes how quickly equilibrium is approached, not the equilibrium composition itself.
why: A catalyst lowers the activation barrier for both forward and reverse reactions. Both rates increase, but their ratio at equilibrium does not change. That is why the faster charge reaches high conversion at a shorter residence time while both curves approach the same ceiling. The catalyst also leaves the reaction enthalpy unchanged. In a real plant, this still matters greatly: a faster catalyst can support more flow through the same reactor. What it cannot buy is a new equilibrium composition at fixed temperature and pressure.
assumes: a catalyst offers a reaction an easier path
equilibrium is where the forward and reverse rates match
answerText: The faster catalyst reaches the same equilibrium conversion in less contact time. Both curves approach the same ceiling, so the catalyst changes rate but not K or the equilibrium yield.

choices: Equilibrium arrives sooner, and the methane the mixture settles at is the same.
More methane at equilibrium, since the easier path favours the forward direction.
Neither the speed nor the amount changes, since the bed is already at equilibrium.
Less heat is released per mole, since the reaction now takes an easier route to get there.
rebuttals: An easier path is easier in both directions at once, which is why the ratio between them does not move.
The bed leaves short of equilibrium at this flow, which is exactly why the speed matters.
Enthalpy is fixed by the starting materials and the products, whatever route joins them.

data.hint: Move the residence-time control across the full range and compare both conversion curves. Look at both how quickly they rise and where they level off.

why_this_format: The misconception is visual and kinetic: a better catalyst changes the approach curve but not its asymptote. A residence-time sweep makes that distinction visible in a way one keyed sentence cannot.
trap_is_satisfied_by: Invented conversion curves are used because the source gives the equilibrium lesson but not a kinetic data series. Both authored curves approach the same 71% ceiling; the higher-activity curve reaches 65% by 3 min while the standard curve needs about 5 min.
player_does: sweep residence time from one to eight minutes
compare the two conversion curves at short contact time
notice that both level off at the same equilibrium ceiling

failure_feedback.action: claiming the higher-activity charge raises the equilibrium yield
failure_feedback.consequence: at long contact time both curves level off at the same conversion
failure_feedback.line: It got there sooner. It did not move where “there” is.

title: The order the cold end has to work in
task: Order the stages of the cold end, warmest to coldest.
scene: Cho is rebuilding the cold end's written procedure after the blockage, and wants the four stages back in the order the stream meets them. Two of the four exist because of what happened on sol 293.
takeaway: Cleaning a stream is cheapest at the warmest temperature that will do it.
why: The stream is cleaned as temperature falls. Each stage sits at a temperature where it can remove one unwanted species before that species harms a colder stage. Compression raises condensation temperatures and can reduce refrigeration demand. Water is removed before it can freeze in the exchanger. Carbon dioxide is trapped at a warmer stage where deposited solid can be managed. Only the cleaned remainder goes to the methane-condensation stage near 112 K. Driving contaminated gas colder wastes energy and creates blockage risk.
assumes: a substance condenses at a temperature that rises with pressure
carbon dioxide turns to solid near 195 K at these pressures

cards: Compress the dry product gas, so everything below condenses at a higher temperature.
Hold the stream at 250 K over a desiccant bed to take the water out as vapour.
Chill to 190 K across the trap, where carbon dioxide leaves as a solid.
Take the remainder to 112 K, where methane runs as a liquid into the tank.

title: The tank that will not freeze
task: Work out how much salt the brine is carrying
scene: The holding tank sat at minus forty overnight and drained as a liquid this morning. Abiola has the analysis: magnesium perchlorate, and a great deal of it. He wants the freezing point that concentration implies.
question: Estimate how far this brine's freezing point falls below that of pure water.
takeaway: In the ideal colligative model, freezing-point depression scales with the number of dissolved particles, not their chemical identity.
why: Dissolved particles lower the chemical potential of liquid water and make freezing occur at a lower temperature. In the ideal colligative model, the size of that shift depends on the number of dissolved particles. Magnesium perchlorate contributes three ions per formula unit, so the van ’t Hoff factor is three in the course calculation. At 8 molal the solution is extremely concentrated, so real ion interactions make the ideal 45 K estimate only a rough magnitude. The calculation still shows why this brine remains liquid far below 0 °C.
assumes: a dissolved salt separates into ions in water
the freezing point of pure water is 273 K

estimate.prompt: The tank holds magnesium perchlorate at 8.0 moles per kilogram of water. Each formula unit gives one magnesium ion and two perchlorate ions.
estimate.question: Estimate how far this brine's freezing point falls below that of pure water.
estimate.relationship: ΔTf = i × Kf × m: the freezing point drops by the particle count i times the water constant Kf times the molality m.
estimate.explanation: The particle count is what matters, so a salt giving three ions counts three times. The boiling-point constant and the molar mass belong to other questions.
estimate.solution: ΔTf = 3 × 1.86 × 8.0 ≈ 45 K below the freezing point of pure water.

equations.about: how far dissolved salt drops a freezing point

title: What the extra volt is doing
task: Account for the voltage above the thermodynamic minimum
scene: The water stack needs 1.23 volts a cell in principle and Achebe runs it at 1.75. The difference is half a kilowatt across the stack, and Demir wants to know whether that energy ends up in the hydrogen.
question: Where does the energy from the extra half-volt a cell end up?
takeaway: A cell run fast costs more per mole than a cell run slowly, and the difference leaves as heat.
why: The thermodynamic minimum voltage pays for the free-energy increase of splitting water. Any voltage above that minimum is overpotential. It is the extra cost of driving useful current through real electrodes and electrolyte. Part of that cost comes from electrical resistance. Part comes from slow electrode steps that need additional driving force. The extra electrical energy ends up mainly as heat in the stack. Hydrogen made at 1.75 V is chemically the same product as hydrogen made closer to the reversible voltage.
assumes: a cell has a minimum voltage set by the thermodynamics of the reaction
electrical power is current times voltage

choices: It leaves the stack as heat, and the hydrogen carries the same energy either way.
It is stored in the hydrogen, which comes out at a higher energy than at 1.23 volts.
It is spent making the reaction go, since below that voltage no water would split.
It goes into warming the water feed, which raises the amount each coulomb can split.
rebuttals: Hydrogen is hydrogen, and the energy stored in it depends on the molecule rather than on the cell that made it.
Below 1.23 volts the reaction genuinely stops, and that first 1.23 is not the half-volt in question.
Some of the heat does warm the feed, and warming water does not change what a coulomb can split.

title: Compute which way it runs
task: Calculate the reaction quotient from the snapshot and compare it with the equilibrium constant.
scene: Herrera freezes the 09:40 gas-analyser screen before the loop has settled. Four partial pressures sit beside the equilibrium constant for 593 K. He wants the direction called before anyone changes a valve.
question: Estimate Q from the four partial pressures. Is the mixture driven forward or backward?
takeaway: Q < K drives the reaction forward, Q > K drives it backward, and Q = K is equilibrium.
why: The reaction quotient uses the same pressure expression as the equilibrium constant, but it uses the mixture that exists right now. Here Q is about 0.016 while K is 0.14. The mixture therefore has too little product relative to equilibrium, so the forward reaction is favoured until Q rises to K. The comparison predicts direction, not speed. A poor catalyst could take a long time to close the gap. Temperature can change K itself; the catalyst cannot.
assumes: for CO₂ + 4H₂ ⇌ CH₄ + 2H₂O, Qp = PCH₄(PH₂O)² / [PCO₂(PH₂)⁴]
Kp is 0.14 at this bed temperature
answerText: Q ≈ 0.016, which is well below K = 0.14. The net reaction therefore runs forward and makes more methane and water.

estimate.prompt: At 593 K: PCH₄ = 1.0 bar, PH₂O = 0.50 bar, PCO₂ = 1.0 bar, PH₂ = 2.0 bar, and Kp = 0.14.
estimate.question: Choose the four partial pressures needed to calculate Qp, then compare the result with Kp.
estimate.relationship: For CO₂ + 4H₂ ⇌ CH₄ + 2H₂O, Qp = PCH₄(PH₂O)² ÷ [PCO₂(PH₂)⁴]. Compare Qp with Kp to get the net direction.
estimate.explanation: Qp ≈ 0.016 and Kp = 0.14. Because Qp is smaller, the mixture moves toward products. Total loop pressure is not substituted separately into Qp.
estimate.solution: Qp = 1.0 × (0.50)² ÷ [1.0 × (2.0)⁴] = 0.0156 < 0.14, so the net direction is forward.

equations.about: reading which way a mixture will move from what is in it now

title: What the tank farm loses standing still
task: Put a number on what the tank loses each sol
scene: Moreau's log shows the oxygen tank losing liquid on sols when nothing is drawn from it. The tank's insulation lets about thirty watts through, and she wants that expressed in kilograms rather than in watts.
question: Estimate the oxygen the tank loses to boil-off each sol.
takeaway: Heat reaching a cryogenic tank is paid for in kilograms rather than in degrees.
why: A cryogenic liquid sits near its boiling point. Heat that enters is therefore spent mainly on vaporising liquid rather than raising its temperature. The required energy per kilogram is the latent heat of vaporisation. That turns an insulation leak directly into a propellant-loss rate. Thirty watts sounds small, but it acts every second of the sol. Over 88,800 seconds it boils away about 12.5 kg of oxygen. Repeated across many sols, a modest heat leak becomes a major production loss.
assumes: a boiling liquid takes in heat without rising in temperature
a sol is about 88,800 seconds long

estimate.prompt: About 30 watts of heat reaches the liquid oxygen tank. Vaporising liquid oxygen takes 213,000 joules per kilogram.
estimate.question: Estimate the oxygen the tank loses to boil-off each sol.
estimate.relationship: Boil-off mass = the heat reaching the tank × the time it reaches it for ÷ the energy needed to vaporise one kilogram.
estimate.explanation: Power times time is energy, and energy divided by the heat of vaporisation is a mass. The boiling point and the molar mass do not enter it.
labels: 213000 J/kg  (heat needed to vaporise liquid oxygen)

title: The reaction that likes being hot
task: Explain the gas nobody asked for
scene: Stern’s assay shows carbon monoxide rising each time the reactor set point is raised. Methane falls by almost the same carbon amount. Kaur has the two candidate reactions on the board and wants the temperature effect explained.
question: Why does the hotter bed make relatively more carbon monoxide?
takeaway: Temperature can change selectivity because competing reactions can have different thermodynamic responses to heating.
why: Competing reactions must be considered separately. The Sabatier reaction is exothermic, so heating shifts its equilibrium toward reactants. The carbon-monoxide-forming side reaction is endothermic, so heating shifts its equilibrium toward products. Both reactions may also become faster as temperature rises. The important point is selectivity: the two equilibrium constants do not move in the same direction. A temperature set point therefore changes not only total conversion, but also how the carbon feed is divided among products.
assumes: free energy combines an enthalpy term with a temperature times an entropy term
a reaction that takes in heat has a positive enthalpy change

choices: Heating favours the reaction that takes heat in and pushes the other back.
Carbon monoxide forms faster than methane does, so a bed running faster makes more of it.
The catalyst changes what it makes once it is above three hundred degrees.
Carbon monoxide is the more stable product, and heat lets the mixture reach it.
rebuttals: Both reactions do speed up with temperature, and speed alone would leave the proportions where they were.
The catalyst offers both paths at every temperature, and it is the two balances that move.
Stability is not one ranking; which product is favoured depends on the temperature being asked about.

equations.e: CO₂ + 4H₂ → CH₄ + 2H₂O,  ΔH = −165 kJ per mole

reading which way a mixture will move from what is in it now

title: Follow the hot spot downstream
task: Probe the temperature profile along the bed and identify which section has stopped contributing.
scene: Nine reactor profiles cover one wall. The hot spot began 4 cm into the bed and now sits 34 cm downstream, while its peak temperature is almost unchanged. Conversion has slipped again this morning.
question: Where has catalyst activity been lost, and what pattern rules out a uniformly weak charge?
takeaway: In an exothermic packed bed, the first active section is revealed by where the temperature rise begins.
why: Reaction heat appears where live catalyst is converting feed. If the whole charge were simply weaker, the heat peak would shrink everywhere. Instead, the peak remains strong and moves downstream. That means the catalyst beyond the front can still work, while the inlet section no longer reacts. Unchanged pressure drop argues against a packing channel, and unchanged feed composition argues against a moving feed ratio. A poison carried with the feed naturally produces this pattern because the first catalyst it meets receives the largest cumulative exposure.
assumes: a reaction gives out its heat where it is happening
a bed can lose activity in one part and keep it in another
answerText: Activity has been lost from the inlet end up to roughly the new reaction front. The unchanged peak strength shows that downstream catalyst still works; the active zone has moved, not weakened uniformly.

choices: The front of the bed has stopped working
The gas is finding a channel through the packing
The feed has changed and the bed is responding to it
The thermocouples have drifted along their sheath since the last service
choiceMechanisms: Dead catalyst passes gas unchanged, so the heat appears wherever live catalyst begins.
A channel lets feed past without contacting the catalyst at all.
A leaner feed reacts further into the bed before it gives out heat.
A sensor problem can move a profile with nothing happening in the bed.
text.headline: The hot spot has walked thirty centimetres down the bed in nine sols, at an unchanged peak temperature.

data.hint: Probe from the inlet downstream. Compare the old and current temperature rise at the same positions, and mark the first position where strong reaction heat still appears.

why_this_format: The original diagnosis names a dead inlet from a headline. PROBE makes the player read the same physical quantity at several bed positions and watch the reaction front move downstream.
trap_is_satisfied_by: Invented intermediate temperature-rise values are used because the source gives only the authored 4 cm and 34 cm hot-spot positions plus an unchanged peak. The current profile keeps the same 34 °C peak but moves it to 34 cm; pressure drop and feed composition remain unchanged.
player_does: probe the old and current temperature rise at several bed positions
find the first position where strong reaction heat remains
use the unchanged peak, feed and pressure drop to reject uniform deactivation and channeling

failure_feedback.consequence: a uniformly weak charge would reduce the peak reaction heat instead of moving a nearly unchanged peak downstream
failure_feedback.line: The peak did not fade. It moved.

title: From amps to kilograms
task: Turn a sol of current into kilograms of hydrogen
scene: One cell in the water stack carried six hundred and forty amps for the whole sol. Achebe wants the hydrogen that represents, worked out from the charge rather than from what the collection line reported.
question: Estimate the hydrogen one cell should produce over a sol.
takeaway: Charge and moles are one measurement in two units, once the electrons per molecule are known.
why: Faraday’s law is charge bookkeeping. Current multiplied by time gives total charge. Dividing by the charge required per mole gives moles of hydrogen. Multiplying by hydrogen’s molar mass gives the product mass. Voltage does not enter this amount calculation; voltage controls the energy cost. The result is a theoretical maximum because it assumes every electron contributes to the intended electrode reaction. Comparing this number with collected hydrogen later gives the current efficiency of the real cell.
assumes: one mole of electrons carries 96,485 coulombs
splitting water to hydrogen takes two electrons per molecule

estimate.prompt: The cell carried 640 amps for 88,800 seconds. Making one mole of hydrogen takes two moles of electrons, which is 192,970 coulombs.
estimate.question: Estimate the hydrogen one cell should produce over a sol.
estimate.relationship: Mass = current × time ÷ the charge needed for one mole of product × the molar mass of that product.
estimate.explanation: Current times time is charge, charge divided by the charge per mole is moles, and moles times the molar mass is grams. The voltage decides the energy bill rather than the amount.
labels: 192970 C/mol  (charge needed for one mole of hydrogen)

title: Four lines off the assay bench
task: Match each assay line to what it says about the loop.

takeaway: An assay is a statement about the process, not only about the bottle it came from.
why: Every line in an assay belongs to a part of the plant. The methane figure is the headline and the least informative. Carbon monoxide is not a contaminant that blew in; it is evidence of a second reaction on the same bed. Unreacted hydrogen is expected in a loop that recycles and would be alarming in one that did not. Water past the drier is a maintenance item that becomes an emergency two hundred metres downstream, at 273 K in the exchanger.
assumes: the loop returns unreacted gas to the reactor inlet
the product stream is dried before it is cooled

choices: The plant is doing its main job, and the arguments all live in the few per cent left over.
A second reaction is running on the same catalyst and taking feed away from the first.
Unreacted feed is going round again, which is the recycle working as it was designed to.
The desiccant is passing some through, and the cold end is where that arrives.
scenarios: Methane at 96.4 per cent of the dry stream.
Carbon monoxide at 0.9 per cent.
Hydrogen at 2.1 per cent.
Water at 400 parts per million after the drier.

why_this_format: The interaction is explicit matching: each assay line maps to one process implication. That is a PROTOCOL-style pairing rather than a CASEBOOK evidence-weighing task.

title: The bed that warns only at the outlet
task: Say what a full polishing column does
scene: The polishing column is a packed bed of ion-exchange resin with a fixed number of sites in it. Abiola has been asked how the plant would know the column was full, and he says the honest answer is that it would not.
question: What happens at the outlet as the exchange front reaches the end of the bed?
takeaway: Ion exchange is limited by capacity; breakthrough is detected by the outlet concentration rising as the loaded front reaches the end.
why: An ion-exchange bed has a finite number of exchange sites. A loading front moves through the resin as those sites fill. The outlet can stay very clean for most of the run, then rise quickly when that front reaches the end. The transition is called breakthrough. It is not perfectly instantaneous, and the exact curve depends on flow and mass transfer. The practical warning is therefore an outlet measurement. Monitoring conductivity often enough lets the plant act before the effluent reaches the inlet concentration.
assumes: an ion-exchange bed swaps unwanted ions for harmless ones
a packed bed holds a finite number of ions
answerText: The outlet stays low until the loading front approaches it, then rises toward the inlet concentration. That breakthrough curve is the warning the plant must monitor.

choices: It rises toward the inlet concentration as the exchange front reaches the outlet.
It rises steadily from the day fresh resin is installed because every captured ion weakens the whole bed equally.
It becomes cleaner just before exhaustion because a heavily loaded resin binds incoming ions more strongly.
It remains at a fixed fraction of the inlet concentration throughout the bed’s life.
rebuttals: Most of the bed can load while the outlet stays low; the rise comes when the loading front approaches the outlet.
A loaded site has less capacity for the next ion, not more.
A capacity-limited bed does not remove one fixed percentage for its whole life.

dayTitle: What the spent charge was carrying
title: One line off the spent charge
task: Which explanation fits every finding?
scene: The spent charge was assayed in three sections: the first twenty millimetres, the middle, and the outlet end. Kaur has the five findings on the board and is no longer sure of her own explanation.
takeaway: Two causes with one symptom are told apart in the material rather than in the plant readings.
why: One material observation settles the main dispute: the nickel particles are still the same size as fresh material. That argues against heat-driven sintering. Trace carbon also makes heavy coking unlikely. A uniformly defective charge should be weak throughout its length, but the outlet section remains active. The remaining pattern fits something arriving with the feed and binding first near the inlet. That mechanism also explains why the active hot zone moved downstream as more of the front section lost usable surface.
assumes: a catalyst can lose activity by heat or by a substance binding to it
heat makes small metal particles merge into larger ones

choices: Something in the feed is binding to the nickel
The bed has been run too hot and the metal has coarsened
Carbon is laying down on the surface and covering it
The charge was already faulty when it was loaded into the reactor
choiceMechanisms: A poison arrives with the feed, so it lands on the first catalyst it meets.
Heat merges small metal particles into larger ones with less surface.
Coke builds up on a catalyst working with carbon-bearing gas.
A bad batch never had the activity the plant assumed it had.
text.headline: The spent charge is dead at the inlet end and lively at the outlet, and the reason is in the material.

why_this_format: The exported row contains candidate explanations but no instrument panel or evidence rows. It therefore plays as a plain four-choice interpretation and should be typed as CHOICE.

dayTitle: What the spent charge was carrying
title: The trace nobody read
task: Date the change in the water
scene: The conductivity of the water leaving the polishing column is logged every sol. The trace runs flat for two hundred and sixty sols, steps up over about four, and runs flat and high from there to this morning.
question: What does the shape of that trace say?
takeaway: A step in a record is a date, and a date turns a fault into a history.
why: The shape of the record carries the history. A fresh exchange bed keeps the outlet conductivity low while unused sites remain. As the loading front reaches the outlet, conductivity rises toward the inlet value and then stays high. That is the breakthrough signature. A saltier feed would also appear in the inlet record, but the inlet stays flat. A sensor reset would produce a much sharper discontinuity. The trace therefore dates breakthrough to about sol 261 and shows prolonged operation after it.
assumes: conductivity rises with the ions dissolved in water
an exchange bed holds a fixed number of ions

choices: The column filled around sol 261 and has passed the feed straight through since.
The feed water got saltier at sol 261 and has stayed that way since.
The conductivity sensor was reset against a standard at sol 261 and reads high now.
The column has been leaking around its seal at a steady rate since it was fitted.
rebuttals: The inlet trace is flat across the whole period, so the water arriving at the column has not changed.
Resetting a sensor moves a trace within a single sol, and this step took four of them.
A steady leak gives a raised, sloping trace from the beginning rather than a flat run and a step.

dayTitle: What the spent charge was carrying
title: Change the time, not the ceiling
task: Hold temperature and pressure fixed, change one operating variable, reverse it, and determine whether the reactor is rate-limited.
scene: Herrera and Sundqvist have argued for a fortnight about whether the hot reactor is at equilibrium or simply short of reaction time. Stern gives them one controlled run before the production schedule resumes.
question: Which controlled change separates a kinetic limit from an equilibrium limit, and does conversion follow it on reversal?
takeaway: Changing residence time at fixed temperature and pressure changes kinetic approach to equilibrium without moving the equilibrium ceiling.
why: Equilibrium at fixed temperature and pressure does not depend on how quickly gas crosses the bed. Kinetics does. Halving the flow doubles residence time while leaving the equilibrium composition unchanged. In this controlled run, conversion rises well beyond repeat scatter and returns when the original flow is restored. That means the reactor had been leaving before the mixture reached its equilibrium ceiling. Changing temperature or pressure would not answer the same question because each would move the equilibrium as well as the reaction rate.
assumes: equilibrium is a ceiling that depends on temperature and pressure
conversion also depends on how long the gas spends in the bed
answerText: Flow is the separating variable. Halving it at fixed temperature and pressure raises conversion from 64% to 69%, and restoring the flow returns it to 64%, showing a rate-limited shortfall.

choices: Halve the flow at the same conditions and see whether conversion rises.
Raise the temperature by twenty degrees and see whether conversion rises.
Raise the pressure by two bar and see whether conversion rises.
Fit a fresh charge and see whether conversion rises.
rebuttals: Temperature moves the ceiling and the speed at once, so a rise proves nothing about which was binding.
Pressure moves both as well, and this reaction's balance is sensitive to it.
A fresh charge changes the rate and cannot distinguish a bed that was already at its ceiling.

equations.about: how long the reaction is given to happen in

data.hint: Change one setting from the baseline, run the assay, then restore it. A useful test changes residence time without moving the equilibrium constant.

why_this_format: The scientific question is causal. CONTROL forces the player to alter residence time while holding the two equilibrium settings fixed and then confirm the response by reversal.
trap_is_satisfied_by: Invented control-run conversions are used because the source specifies the discriminating experiment but not its result. Halving flow moves conversion by 5 percentage points against 0.7-point repeat noise, or 7.1× noise; restoring 85 L/min returns the response to 64%.

halve the flow and read conversion
restore the baseline flow before naming the limiting mechanism

title: Bringing a charge into service
task: Order the four operations for bringing the charge into service.
scene: The fresh charge arrives as nickel oxide on alumina, which is not a catalyst yet. Kaur has four operations written out and wants them in an order she can hand to a technician at three in the morning.
takeaway: A part that cannot be replaced is proved at low rate before it is trusted at full rate.
why: Each operation makes the next one possible or safer. Nitrogen purge removes oxygen before hot hydrogen enters the reactor. Reduction must then convert nickel oxide into active nickel metal. A low-flow light-off test checks whether the new charge is active before full production feed is committed. Only after that should the plant run a matched comparison against a known good charge. The comparison creates a quantitative baseline for the next crew instead of leaving them only a verbal impression of performance.

hydrogen at temperature will reduce a metal oxide

title: One improvement, four candidates
task: Fund the change that would most alter what the plant does next.
scene: The station has parts and crew time for one improvement. One catalyst charge is already lost, and there is no spare after the new one. Achebe puts four candidates on the board before anyone starts cutting pipe.
takeaway: The work worth doing first is the work that would have caught the fault nobody caught.
why: The failure was not that the plant lacked a measurement. Conductivity was recorded every sol. The failure was that no rule turned the measurement into an action. A feed-water alarm would have made the breakthrough visible while the catalyst could still be protected. A second polishing column adds capacity but still needs a trigger for changeover. Extra array power does not address the fault, and the catalyst already has several temperature probes. The highest-leverage change closes the gap between an existing signal and an irreversible consequence.

the plant has no spare catalyst charge after this one

Fit a conductivity monitor with an alarm on the reactor feed water.
Add a fourth panel string to the array to raise the power available.
Install a second temperature probe in the catalyst bed.

title: The tank pressure that is not a leak
task: Decide whether a rising pressure is a leak
scene: The methane tank has climbed about 0.3 bar a sol for four sols. The mass in the tank is unchanged across the same four sols, and Moreau is being asked whether to vent it.
question: The pressure is rising and the mass is not falling. What is happening?
takeaway: Pressure in a cryogenic tank is a reading of temperature until the mass says otherwise.
why: A tank holding liquid and vapour together sits near the vapour pressure set by its temperature. Pressure is therefore a sensitive thermometer while both phases remain present. Here the mass has stayed constant for four sols, so a significant leak or sustained venting is not supported by the inventory. The rising pressure instead points to warming. The response is to find the added heat — insulation, a conducting valve or a refrigeration problem — rather than venting propellant merely because the pressure rose.
assumes: a liquid in a closed tank sits under the pressure of its own vapour
vapour pressure rises steeply with temperature

choices: The contents are warming, and the vapour pressure is following the temperature up.
Gas is escaping through a leak even though the measured tank mass is unchanged.
The liquid is boiling away fast enough to raise pressure without changing the tank inventory.
The gauge must have drifted because pressure cannot change at constant mass.
rebuttals: A leak large enough to explain the pressure trend should also appear as a mass loss; the inventory is flat.
Sustained boil-off or venting changes the liquid inventory unless the vapour is retained, and the pressure rise still requires warming.
Constant mass does not imply constant pressure when temperature changes.

title: The bill for a kilogram of hydrogen
task: Put a number on what the hydrogen costs
scene: Demir is closing the sol’s energy ledger. The stacks made 6.9 kg of hydrogen. He wants their electrical energy use written beside the array output before he signs the sheet.
question: Estimate the electrical energy the stacks spent making hydrogen this sol.
takeaway: What a product costs to make and what it stores are two different numbers, and the gap is the price of running at a rate.
why: A kilogram of hydrogen has two useful energy numbers. One is the chemical energy stored in the hydrogen itself. The other is the electrical energy this stack spends to make that kilogram. The second is larger because real cells operate above the reversible voltage. That difference becomes heat and other losses in the electrolysis system. Here the stack uses about 55 kWh/kg while hydrogen stores about 39.4 kWh/kg. Using the stored-energy number as the production cost would understate the electrical bill substantially.

a stack costs more energy per kilogram than the hydrogen itself carries

title: The space left at the top
task: Say how full a cryogenic tank may be filled
scene: Bhatt's loading procedure stops the methane tank at ninety-five per cent by volume. Moreau has been asked why the remaining five per cent is not simply more propellant, with the window as close as it is.
question: Why is the flight tank filled to ninety-five per cent rather than full?
takeaway: A cryogenic tank is designed around what happens to it between filling and use.
why: A cryogenic tank always contains some vapour because heat continues to enter. The gas space above the liquid is the ullage. It gives newly formed vapour room before pressure reaches the relief setting. Filling the tank completely with liquid removes that buffer. Heating then causes liquid expansion and vapour formation to drive pressure upward quickly. The relief system must vent material to protect the tank. Leaving planned ullage therefore prevents a small heat input from immediately becoming a propellant-loss event before the vehicle uses the fuel.
assumes: a liquid at its boiling point turns to vapour when heat reaches it
a closed vessel has a pressure it is rated to

choices: Vapour from boil-off needs somewhere to go, or the tank pressure climbs against its rating.
Liquid methane expands as it cools further in the tank and would split a full one.
A full tank cannot be measured, since the gauge floats on the liquid surface.
The pump cannot draw from a tank with no gas above the liquid to push it out.
rebuttals: Liquid methane in a tank sits at its boiling point and is not cooling further.
The gauge on this tank reads by pressure and temperature and does not need a surface to float on.
The pump is fed by pressure from the tank's own vapour, and five per cent is not what makes that possible.

title: Close the carbon pass
task: Close the 100-mole carbon ledger for one pass, then decide which carbon is lost and which is recycled.

question: Where are all 100 carbon moles after one pass, and what does that imply for overall methane yield after repeated recycle?
takeaway: Per-pass conversion counts what reacts now; overall conversion counts what is eventually recovered after unreacted feed is recycled.
why: A one-pass conversion of 64% does not mean 36% of the feed is lost. The carbon ledger shows 64 moles leaving as methane, two as carbon monoxide and 34 returning as unreacted carbon dioxide. The recycle term is therefore inventory, not waste. If the same selectivity holds over repeated passes, the returned carbon keeps getting another chance. The ultimate split approaches the ratio of the irreversible products: 64/(64+2), or about 97% methane, with about 3% ending as carbon monoxide.
assumes: the recycle loop returns unreacted gas to the inlet
every carbon atom entering the bed leaves it in something
answerText: The pass closes as 64 CH₄ + 2 CO + 34 recycled CO₂ = 100 carbon moles. Recycle makes the overall methane fraction approach about 64/(64+2) ≈ 97%, not 64%.

Sixty-four per cent of it, since that is what one pass through the bed converts.
A third of it, since the unreacted gas has to be vented to stop it building up.
Two per cent of it is lost and the rest is unknowable without a second measurement.
rebuttals: Sixty-four per cent is the per-pass figure, and the recycle is what makes the overall figure different from it.
Unreacted feed is the loop's own working inventory rather than something to vent.
The count is complete: a hundred moles in, and a hundred accounted for on the way out.

dayTitle: Forty per cent of the sun
title: What the dust leaves of the sun
task: Work out how much sunlight is reaching the panels
scene: Petrov has the optical depth from the station's own sun sensor: 2.4, against 0.4 on a clear sol. Above the dust the beam would deliver four hundred and ninety watts to each square metre of panel.
question: Estimate the direct beam reaching a panel through this dust.
takeaway: Dust does not dim a beam in proportion; it multiplies it down, so each unit of depth costs more than the last.
why: Dust attenuation is multiplicative. Each additional unit of optical depth removes the same fraction of the beam that remains. That is why a change from τ = 0.4 to τ = 2.4 is much worse than subtracting two equal pieces of sunlight. The direct beam falls to under a tenth of the above-dust value. The array still receives some scattered light from the sky, so direct-beam loss is not the same as total array output. The exponential relation describes only the unscattered beam.
assumes: each unit of optical depth cuts a beam by a further factor
a beam is attenuated as an exponential of the depth it passes through

estimate.prompt: Above the dust the beam is 490 watts a square metre. The station's sun sensor reports an optical depth of 2.4.
estimate.question: Estimate the direct beam reaching a panel through this dust.
estimate.relationship: Transmitted beam = the beam above the dust × e raised to minus the optical depth: each unit of depth divides the beam by a further factor of about 2.7.
estimate.explanation: The exponential is why a storm is so much worse than it looks. The panel efficiency and the array area turn this into kilowatts, and are a later step.
estimate.solution: 490 × e^(−2.4) ≈ 44 W per square metre of direct beam.

dayTitle: Forty per cent of the sun
title: What the station stops doing
task: Build a plan for the power there is
scene: The dust storm has cut the sol from about 2,000 kilowatt-hours to 430. Tank refrigeration is already drawing power, and six other demands are queued. Demir and Wells want the sacrifices written down before breakers are opened.
question: Four hundred and thirty kilowatt-hours. Build the sol's plan, and know what it stops the station being able to say.
takeaway: Loads are ranked by what stopping them costs to undo, rather than by what they draw.
why: The power plan should rank loads by the cost of stopping them. Digging is recoverable because the ground remains available. Batteries can recharge on the next clear sol. Electrolysis can be made up later if schedule margin remains. Cryogenic refrigeration is different. When it stops, heat keeps entering the tanks and already-made propellant boils away. That loss cannot be recovered without making new propellant later. Habitat power is protected separately. The scarce pool should therefore preserve irreversible assets before funding work that can simply be deferred.
assumes: stopping a process can be reversible or costly to reverse
a cryogenic tank warms up when its refrigerator stops
answerText: Keep the protected habitat bus and cryogenic refrigeration inside the 430 kWh limit. Then choose at most one substantial optional job. The jobs left unfunded are part of the answer.

data.hint: Protect the load whose loss is irreversible. The live board shows which operating question each optional load answers and which ones your plan gives up.

answers.label: Keep already-made cryogenic propellant from boiling away
Recharge the storm battery reserve today

trap_is_satisfied_by: Invented item-level kWh costs are used because the source provides only the 430 kWh pool and the qualitative load ranking. The listed costs total 1,230 kWh against 430 available. Refrigeration costs 250 kWh, leaving 180, so the plan can preserve cryogens and fund at most one substantial optional load. Habitat is protected at cost 0 as required by the format.

failure_feedback.action: dropping refrigeration to keep electrolysis running
failure_feedback.consequence: new hydrogen is made while previously produced cryogenic propellant boils away and cannot be recovered
failure_feedback.line: Do not spend today’s power remaking what we vented yesterday.

dayTitle: Forty per cent of the sun
title: Running the plant with no digging
task: Decide what the water plant does with no drill
scene: The drill is off and the hopper is empty. The holding tank still contains 1,100 litres, while the reactor draws about 60 litres per sol. Abiola is asked whether the whole water plant must stop.
question: What lets the reactor keep running through a storm with the drill stopped?
takeaway: A buffer between two steps is what lets one of them stop without the other one noticing.
why: Two buffers separate the reactor from daily drilling. The first is stored water: 1,100 litres at 60 litres per sol is about eighteen sols of inventory. That is longer than the storms recorded at this site. The second is process recycle. The Sabatier reaction produces water, and the plant condenses and returns part of that stream. Those two buffers let extraction pause without forcing an immediate reactor shutdown. They also show why plant reliability depends on inventories between steps, not only on the machines themselves.
assumes: the reactor's water demand is met from a holding tank rather than from the drill directly
the Sabatier reaction makes water as well as methane

choices: The holding tank, plus the water the reaction itself gives back into the loop.
The condenser, which pulls water vapour out of the atmosphere at six millibars.
The polishing column, which stores clean water inside its resin bed.
Nothing does; the reactor has to stop with the drill and restart afterwards.
rebuttals: The atmosphere here holds almost no water vapour, and the condenser works on the hopper stream instead.
An exchange bed holds ions rather than water, and it holds no useful volume.
Restarting a cold reactor costs a sol of production, which is exactly what the buffer exists to avoid.

title: Follow the heat to the sky
task: Build the refrigerator heat path in order and identify the transfer that dust has made limiting.
scene: Oxygen boil-off has jumped from 12 to 26 kilograms a sol since the storm. Moreau opens the refrigeration schematic beside the tank. Jacket pressure is normal, while the compressor is already at its current limit.
question: Trace the heat from the liquid oxygen to its final sink. Which required transfer is now governing the loss?
takeaway: A refrigerator can lose capacity because heat cannot leave its warm end, even when the compressor and insulation are intact.
why: The refrigerator does not destroy heat. It moves heat from the tank into the refrigerant. Compressor work then raises the refrigerant temperature enough for heat rejection. The condenser transfers that heat to the radiator, which must radiate it to the sky. The vacuum jacket is a separate path for unwanted heat to enter the tank. Its normal pressure makes that path less likely here. Dust weakens the final radiator-to-sky transfer, so the cold end warms even while the compressor works at its limit.
assumes: a refrigerator has to reject its heat somewhere
dust settles on any surface left out in a storm
answerText: The governing link is heat rejection from the dusty radiator to the sky. The compressor is working, and the jacket is intact, but the final heat-transfer step has lost capacity.

choices: Dust on the radiator is stopping the refrigerator rejecting its heat
The tank insulation has been damaged by the storm
The refrigerator compressor is failing
The tank has been overfilled and is venting the excess
choiceMechanisms: A machine that cannot dump heat to the sky cannot hold its cold end down.
A failed vacuum jacket lets heat straight into the liquid.
A worn machine draws less current and delivers less cooling.
An overfull tank relieves itself until the ullage is restored.
text.headline: Boil-off has doubled since the storm, with the tank's insulation intact.

title: Comparing two charges honestly
task: Set the terms of a fair comparison
scene: Kaur wants the new charge compared against the sol-270 run before it is trusted with the rest of the season. The plant is at a different temperature, flow and pressure than it was on sol 270.
question: What has to be true for a comparison between two charges to mean anything?
takeaway: A comparison is worth what its matched conditions are worth.
why: Conversion depends on several variables at once. Temperature, pressure and flow are operating settings, while catalyst condition is the property being compared. If the settings differ between two runs, the comparison mixes catalyst performance with operating effects. Matching those settings removes the main alternative explanations. The remaining conversion difference can then be attributed more credibly to the charge. Running each catalyst at its own best condition answers a different question and produces two results that cannot be cleanly subtracted.
assumes: conversion depends on temperature, pressure, flow and the catalyst together
a comparison is only about the variable that was deliberately changed

choices: Temperature, pressure and flow are set to the sol-270 values before conversion is read.
Both charges are run at whatever conditions produce their best conversion.
The comparison uses a whole sol of production from each charge.
Both are compared at the same time of sol, so the ambient conditions match.
rebuttals: Best-for-each conditions produce two numbers that cannot be compared, since the settings differ along with the charge.
A whole sol of each is more data about an unmatched comparison, which does not repair it.
Ambient conditions outside barely reach a reactor held at 593 K, and the loop's own settings are what matter.

title: Which of the three cannot wait
task: Rank three faults against each other
scene: The three problems are on the board with the power to fix one of them today. Wells wants the order and the grounds for it in the log before anybody starts work.
question: Which of the three is dealt with first?
takeaway: What cannot be undone goes first, whatever is loudest.
why: Rank by what a delay costs and whether it can be recovered. Boil-off is a loss of a thing already made, running at fourteen extra kilograms a sol, and no later work brings those kilograms back. Batteries recharge on the next clear sol. A comparison run is information, and information waits at no cost provided the bed is watched. Only one of the three is spending an asset while it is queued, and that is the one that goes first.
assumes: propellant vented from a tank cannot be recovered
a comparison run and a battery charge can both be done later

choices: The radiator, since every sol of doubled boil-off is propellant that leaves for good.
The battery bank, since another storm without reserve would stop the whole station.
The charge comparison, since the season's production depends on knowing the bed is good.
Whichever can be finished today, since a finished job is worth more than a started one.
rebuttals: The battery bank refills on the next clear sol at no permanent cost, and one has been forecast.
The comparison matters and loses nothing by waiting two sols, since the bed is under watch.
Choosing by what fits in a sol ranks by convenience and ignores what each delay is costing.

title: The line that fails
task: Match each assay line to what it means for the vehicle.
scene: The loading crew is waiting at the methane umbilical. Bhatt has four assay lines beside four flight limits. Three are inside specification; one is not. Herrera wants the consequence named before the transfer valve opens.
takeaway: A specification is a list of chemical limits tied to different downstream consequences, not a single purity score.
why: A specification is not one overall purity score. Each line protects a different downstream function. Water is the failure here: 400 ppm is eight times a 50 ppm limit. At cryogenic valve temperatures, that water can become solid and interfere with moving hardware. Carbon monoxide and carbon dioxide are still inside their stated limits. If either rose too far, it would create a different consequence. The vehicle therefore needs every assay line interpreted against its own limit and failure mode before loading begins.
assumes: water freezes at a temperature the vehicle's valves reach in use
carbon monoxide does not burn to give the energy methane does

choices: Inside the limit, and the margin is thin enough to be worth watching on the next batch.
Eight times the limit, and it freezes in a valve at the temperature that valve runs at.
Inside the limit; it is ballast that costs a little performance and does no damage.
Inside the limit, and it freezes out in the tank rather than in a moving part.
scenarios: Methane at 99.1 per cent against a limit of 99.0.
Water at 400 parts per million against a limit of 50.
Carbon monoxide at 0.5 per cent against a limit of 1.0.
Carbon dioxide at 0.2 per cent against a limit of 0.5.

why_this_format: The row is a four-way matching task: each assay line is paired with its operational meaning. PROTOCOL matches the interaction already encoded by its scenarios and choices better than CASEBOOK.

title: How much oxygen a tonne of methane needs
task: Work out how much oxygen goes with the methane
scene: Bhatt wants the oxygen mass checked independently before the loading order is written. Methane burns with oxygen two moles to one, and the vehicle carries six point six tonnes of fuel.
question: Estimate the mass of oxygen needed for each kilogram of methane burned.
takeaway: A mole ratio is not a mass ratio until both molar masses have been applied.
why: A balanced equation gives a mole ratio, while tanks are filled by mass. Complete methane combustion uses two moles of oxygen for every mole of methane. Two moles of O₂ have a mass of 64 g, while one mole of CH₄ has a mass of 16 g. The stoichiometric oxygen-to-fuel mass ratio is therefore 4:1. A rocket engine may deliberately operate away from that exact ratio for performance reasons. That design choice does not change the stoichiometric calculation the loading team must understand.
assumes: a balanced equation gives the mole ratio for a reaction
a molar mass converts a number of moles into a mass

estimate.prompt: Burning methane completely takes two moles of oxygen per mole of methane. Oxygen is 32.0 g per mole and methane is 16.0.
estimate.question: Estimate the mass of oxygen needed for each kilogram of methane burned.
estimate.relationship: Mass ratio = the mole ratio from the balanced equation × the molar mass of the oxidiser ÷ the molar mass of the fuel.
estimate.explanation: The mole ratio is 2 to 1 and the mass ratio is 4 to 1, since oxygen is twice as heavy a molecule. The engine actually runs below this, which is a design choice rather than an arithmetic one.
estimate.solution: 2 × 32.0 ÷ 16.0 = 4.0 kilograms of oxygen for each kilogram of methane.
labels: 2  (moles of oxygen per mole of methane)
