title: Push the stack until heat wins
task: Sweep stack current and find where extra hydrogen production outruns the cooling loop.
scene: Sundqvist asks for 20% above the stack’s 640-amp rated point for the final sols. Achebe opens the current control and cooling display. More hydrogen is useful only while stack heat stays inside what the loop can remove.
question: How far can current be raised before waste heat crosses the cooling capacity, and why does product keep rising after that point?
takeaway: Faraday production rises with current, while ohmic heating can rise roughly with current squared and set a thermal operating limit.
why: Faraday’s law has no built-in current ceiling: more charge gives proportionally more hydrogen. The penalty is the voltage above the thermodynamic minimum. When ohmic loss dominates, the waste power grows approximately as current squared. A 20% current increase can therefore produce about 20% more hydrogen while creating roughly 44% more resistive heat. The cooling loop, seals and electrolyte temperature set the practical ceiling. The sweep makes the trade visible: the chemical output keeps rising even after the hardware has left its safe thermal region.
assumes: the product a cell makes is proportional to the charge it passes
the voltage above the minimum leaves the cell as heat
answerText: In this authored sweep, about 704 A is still inside the cooling capacity and 736 A is not. The requested 768 A would make about 20% more hydrogen but roughly 44% more ohmic heat than the rated point.

choices: The heat the cooling loop can carry away, since the wasted voltage rises with the current.
Faraday's constant, which fixes how many moles a cell can pass in a sol.
The water supply, since a cell can split no more than it is fed.
The pressure in the hydrogen collection line, which rises with the production rate.
rebuttals: Faraday's constant converts charge into moles and does not cap the charge itself.
Water feed is a limit worth checking and this hall has buffer enough for the requested rate.
Collection pressure is held by a regulator and does not rise with production.

equations.about: Faraday's law: charge into kilograms

data.hint: Sweep current and compare the hydrogen-production curve with the waste-heat curve. The cooling capacity is fixed; do not treat a rising product line as proof that the operating point is acceptable.

series.label: Ohmic waste heat relative to rated

why_this_format: The misconception is a trade-off hidden by one current number. SWEEP lets the player see linear Faraday production and faster-growing heat on the same control axis, then locate the cooling-limited operating region.
trap_is_satisfied_by: Invented cooling headroom is used because the source gives the rated 640 A point and the 20%-over request but no cooling-loop number. At 704 A the modeled ohmic heat is 121% of rated, below the 125% cooling capacity; at 736 A it is 132% and fails. At 768 A it reaches 144%.

compare hydrogen output with waste heat at each setting
stop at the last point that remains below the cooling capacity

dayTitle: What the next crew is told
title: What to leave running
task: Fund what the next crew should inherit.
scene: Only two improvements can be left in place for the crew arriving 300 sols from now. Wells and Demir have four candidates on the final board. The failed catalyst charge is on the floor beside them.
takeaway: What outlives a crew is what somebody made automatic before they left.
why: The best inheritance is a system that turns a known failure mode into an automatic response. The conductivity alarm closes the exact gap that let breakthrough continue unnoticed. The standing order for lead-and-lag column changeover tells the next crew what to do when that signal arrives. Spare thermocouples are useful but the bed already has temperature coverage, and a second sun sensor does not address the failure that consumed the catalyst. Together, alarm plus procedure connect measurement, threshold and action without requiring this crew’s memory.
assumes: the fault that cost this season went undetected because nothing measured it
the next crew arrives without anybody from this one
answerText: Leave the feed-water conductivity alarm and the standing lead/lag changeover rule. Together they detect breakthrough and tell the next crew what action follows.

proposals: An alarm on feed-water conductivity, wired to the plant panel rather than to a log.
A written standing order for changing the lead polishing column at breakthrough.
A spare set of thermocouples for the catalyst bed.
A second sun sensor at the far end of the array.
text.evidence: This season lost thirty-eight sols of production to a measurement that was taken every sol, logged every sol, and read by nobody. The bed already carries four thermocouples and the array has one sun sensor that has never disagreed with the sky.

dayTitle: What the next crew is told
title: Write the rule before the trace moves
task: Set the warning and column-swap thresholds, then replay the historic conductivity rise without changing them.
scene: Abiola is writing a rule for a crew he will never meet. He loads last season’s conductivity trace into the alarm simulator. Once the replay starts, the thresholds are locked and the values run forward.
question: Where should warning and changeover trigger so the fresh column is in service before feed water leaves the accepted range?
takeaway: A breakthrough threshold must be written before the rise and early enough to cover the action’s lead time.
why: The outlet can remain near baseline while the exchange front is still inside the bed, then rise quickly as the front reaches the end. A threshold is useful only if the response can finish before the water leaves specification. Here changeover takes one update. Triggering at twice baseline completes the swap while the next point is still 2.6 times baseline. Waiting for 2.6 completes it after the trace has crossed the 3.0 limit. Precommitting the rule prevents the next crew from turning hindsight into policy.
assumes: an exchange bed reaches breakthrough without warning
a lead and lag pair lets one bed be changed while the other works
answerText: Warn near 1.6× clean-baseline conductivity and start the lead/lag swap at 2.0×. With one-update lead time, the fresh bed is online before the replay crosses the 3.0× limit.

cards: Read the conductivity at the outlet of the lead column against yesterday's figure.
Move the lag column into the lead position when that figure has doubled.
Fit a fresh column into the vacant lag position within the same sol.
Enter the change and the conductivity at the moment of it in the plant record.

data.hint: Set both rules before release. The swap takes one update to complete. The accepted-water limit on this normalized replay is 3.0 times the clean baseline.

stages.label: Move lag column into lead service

why_this_format: The sequence screen tells the player the standing order after the fact. TRIGGER makes them encode the actual breakthrough rule before the historical trace moves and live with the lead-time consequence.
trap_is_satisfied_by: Invented normalized replay values and warning lead time are used because the source gives the historical step shape and the “double conductivity” rule but no raw conductivity units. The scale reaches 6.0 above the stream maximum 4.5. A swap triggered at 2.0 completes at 2.6, below the 3.0 limit; waiting for 2.6 completes at 3.4 and fails.

release the historic breakthrough trace
check whether the one-update changeover finishes before the accepted-water limit is crossed

failure_feedback.consequence: the one-update changeover finishes after conductivity has crossed the 3.0× accepted-water limit

dayTitle: What the next crew is told
title: The honest claim about the bed
task: State what is known about the catalyst and what is not
scene: Kaur is writing the final catalyst handover. The bed has run for five sols at one set of conditions using water from a fresh polishing column. It is the last charge available on the station.
question: What is the honest claim to hand over about this charge?
takeaway: The strength of a claim is set by what was varied while it was being tested.
why: A claim is limited by the conditions under which the evidence was collected. Five sols at one set point on clean water support a narrow statement about that operating window. They do not establish performance at other temperatures or flows. They also do not test resistance to chloride because chloride was intentionally absent after the column change. A useful handover keeps those conditions attached to the claim. The next crew can then tell whether a future observation is a replication of this result or a genuinely new test.
assumes: a claim is limited by the conditions it was tested under
a poison accumulates over time rather than acting at once

choices: It matches the sol-270 charge at matched conditions over five sols, on polished water.
It performs as well as any charge the station has run, on the evidence available.
It is unaffected by chloride, since conversion has held since the column was changed.
Its behaviour cannot be stated, since five sols is too short a run to say anything.
rebuttals: A comparison against every charge the station has run was not made, and two of them were never assayed.
Chloride was absent throughout, so the run says nothing about what the charge does when it is present.
Five sols supports a narrow claim rather than none at all, and the narrow claim is worth writing down.
